p.src: Which Velocity Have We Measured?

u.src: Which Velocity Have We Measured?
en: Which Velocity Have We Measured?

p.src:
Suppose a first position measurement locates a particle only within a region of width $\delta$. Wait a time $T$, make a second measurement with the same resolution, and let the centers of the two regions be separated by $L$. The inferred average velocity is $v_{\mathrm{avg}}\simeq \frac{L}{T},
 \qquad
 \Delta v_{\mathrm{avg}}\sim \frac{\delta}{T}.$ Numerical factors in the second estimate are unimportant. By making $T$ large, we can make $\delta/T$ as small as we please. Have we measured position to accuracy $\delta$ and velocity almost exactly?

p.src: Trying to verify the result does not restore the missing information. Repeating the procedure changes the momentum again by an amount of order $\hbar/\delta$. Classical physics permits an ideal limit in which position is observed ever more gently while the velocity is left alone. Quantum mechanics does not. This is the point of the uncertainty principle, and with it settled we can begin the mathematics needed for states.

p.src: The One-Dimensional Model: Complex Numbers

u.src: The One-Dimensional Model: Complex Numbers
en: The One-Dimensional Model: Complex Numbers

p.src:
The next subject is dry, but it is not difficult. We need a quick review of complex numbers only to establish notation. Write $z=x+iy,
 \qquad
 z^*=x-iy,
 \qquad
 i^2=-1.$ In the complex plane, conjugation reflects a point across the real axis. Complex numbers can be added and multiplied by arbitrary complex scalars, so $\mathbb C$ is itself a one-dimensional complex vector space. It is the simplest model of the structures we shall use.

The next subject is dry, but it is not difficult. We need a quick review of complex numbers only to establish notation. Write $z=x+iy,
 \qquad
 z^*=x-iy,
 \qquad
 i^2=-1.$ In the complex plane, conjugation reflects a point across the real axis. Complex numbers can be added and multiplied by arbitrary complex scalars, so $\mathbb C$ is itself a one-dimensional complex vector space. It is the simplest model of the structures we shall use.

p.src:
In this one-dimensional model, regard $z$ as a ket and $z^*$ as its corresponding bra. Complex conjugation exchanges the two. If $z_1=x_1+iy_1,
 \qquad
 z_2=x_2+iy_2,$ then $\begin{aligned}
 z_1z_2
 &= (x_1x_2-y_1y_2)+i(x_1y_2+y_1x_2),\\
 (z_1z_2)^*
 &=z_1^*z_2^*.
 \end{aligned}$ For scalar numbers the factors commute. It is nevertheless useful to write the related identity $(z_1^*z_2)^*=z_2^*z_1,$ because the reversal of bra and ket will survive when the intervening objects no longer commute.

p.src: What Makes a Complex Vector Space?

u.src: What Makes a Complex Vector Space?
en: What Makes a Complex Vector Space?

p.src: A complex vector space is a collection of objects that may be added and multiplied by complex numbers without leaving the collection. If $|A\rangle$ and $|B\rangle$ are vectors and $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$, then $\alpha|A\rangle+\beta|B\rangle$ must be another vector in the same space. The vectors need not be arrows. What matters is the algebra of addition and scalar multiplication.

What matters is the algebra of addition and scalar multiplication.

p.src: Several near-examples make the definition precise. Ordinary arrows form a real vector space, but not a complex vector space unless an additional rule for multiplication by $i$ is supplied. The real numbers form a real vector space, not a complex one. The positive real numbers do not even form a real vector space: multiplying a positive number by $-1$ leaves the set.

p.src: Functions and Columns

u.src: Functions and Columns
en: Functions and Columns

p.src:
Complex-valued functions of a real variable form a complex vector space. If $\psi(x)$ and $\phi(x)$ are such functions, then $(\alpha\psi+\beta\phi)(x)
 =\alpha\psi(x)+\beta\phi(x)$ is another complex-valued function.

en:
Complex-valued functions of a real variable form a complex vector space. If $\psi(x)$ and $\phi(x)$ are such functions, then $(\alpha\psi+\beta\phi)(x)

p.src:
A column vector is the same idea with a discrete argument. For four components, $|a\rangle=
 \begin{pmatrix}a_1\\a_2\\a_3\\a_4\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 |b\rangle=
 \begin{pmatrix}b_1\\b_2\\b_3\\b_4\end{pmatrix},$ and $\alpha|a\rangle+\beta|b\rangle
 =
 \begin{pmatrix}
  \alpha a_1+\beta b_1\\
  \alpha a_2+\beta b_2\\
  \alpha a_3+\beta b_3\\
  \alpha a_4+\beta b_4
 \end{pmatrix}.$ The index $1,2,3,4$ plays the role of a discrete coordinate.

p.src: Dimension and Spanning

u.src: Dimension and Spanning
en: Dimension and Spanning

p.src: The dimension of a vector space is the minimum number of independent vectors needed to span it. One nonzero vector spans a line. Two noncollinear vectors span a plane: every vector $|v\rangle$ in that plane can be written $|v\rangle=r_1|v_1\rangle+r_2|v_2\rangle.$ A third vector in the same plane adds no new direction, because it is already a linear combination of the first two. In three dimensions we need three noncoplanar vectors.

p.src:
Columns with four components form a vector space of dimension four. One convenient basis is $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},
 \quad
 \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},
 \quad
 \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix},
 \quad
 \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.$ Remove the last column and no linear combination can produce a nonzero fourth component. By contrast, one-component columns are just complex numbers and form a one-dimensional complex space.

p.src:
The space of smooth complex functions has no finite spanning set; it is infinite-dimensional. The details of bases in infinite-dimensional spaces will not concern us yet. For now, the essential point is that functions and columns are both concrete representations of abstract vectors: $\psi(x)\longmapsto|\psi\rangle,
 \qquad
 \begin{pmatrix}\psi_1\\ \psi_2\\ \vdots\end{pmatrix}
 \longmapsto|\psi\rangle.$

p.src: Bras, Kets, and the Dual Space

u.src: Bras, Kets, and the Dual Space
en: Bras, Kets, and the Dual Space

p.src:
To every ket $|A\rangle$ we associate a bra $\langle A|$. A bra is a linear functional: when it acts on a ket, it produces a complex number. Once an inner product has been chosen, the Riesz correspondence identifies each ket with a bra antilinearly. In finite-dimensional coordinates this is the familiar conjugate transpose: $|A\rangle=
 \begin{pmatrix}a_1\\a_2\\ \vdots\\a_d\end{pmatrix}
 \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
 \langle A|=
 \begin{pmatrix}a_1^*&a_2^*&\cdots&a_d^*\end{pmatrix}.$ For a function, the corresponding bra is represented by the conjugate function $\psi^*(x)$.

p.src: Inner Products

u.src: Inner Products
en: Inner Products

p.src:
For ordinary real vectors, the dot product is $\mathbf a\mathbin{\boldsymbol\cdot}\mathbf b
 =|\mathbf a|\,|\mathbf b|\cos\theta
 =\sum_i a_i b_i.$ The inner product $\langle A|B\rangle$ is its complex counterpart. We use the convention standard in physics: it is linear in the ket and conjugate-linear in the bra. Thus $\begin{aligned}
 \langle A|(\beta B+\gamma C)\rangle
 &=\beta\langle A|B\rangle+\gamma\langle A|C\rangle,\\
 \langle \alpha A|B\rangle
 &=\alpha^*\langle A|B\rangle.
 \end{aligned}$ It also obeys conjugate symmetry, $\langle A|B\rangle=\langle B|A\rangle^*.$ Setting $B=A$ shows that $\langle A|A\rangle$ is real. Positivity is an additional axiom: $\langle A|A\rangle\geq 0,
 \qquad
 \langle A|A\rangle=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ |A\rangle=0.$ It is not a consequence of conjugate symmetry alone. Relativity supplies a useful warning: the Minkowski metric admits positive, negative, and null norms, so it is not an inner product in this positive-definite sense.

p.src: Orthonormal Bases and Components

u.src: Orthonormal Bases and Components
en: Orthonormal Bases and Components

p.src:
Choose $d$ vectors $\{|b_i\rangle\}_{i=1}^{d}$ in a $d$-dimensional space. They are normalized when $\langle b_i|b_i\rangle=1$, with no sum on $i$, and mutually orthogonal when $\langle b_i|b_j\rangle=0$ for $i\neq j$. Both statements are contained in $\langle b_i|b_j\rangle=\delta_{ij},
 \qquad
 \delta_{ij}=
 \begin{cases}
  1,&i=j,\\
  0,&i\neq j.
 \end{cases}$ An orthonormal set of $d$ vectors in a $d$-dimensional space is a basis. The columns in Eq.  provide the standard example. Their corresponding bras are rows. A blackboard slip between the row and column forms was caught in the room; the corrected notation is the one used here.

p.src:
Any vector can be expanded in the basis: $|v\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{d}v_i|b_i\rangle.$ Multiply from the left by $\langle b_j|$: $\begin{aligned}
 \langle b_j|v\rangle
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{d}v_i\langle b_j|b_i\rangle\\
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{d}v_i\delta_{ji}
 =v_j.
 \end{aligned}$ The component $v_j$ is the inner product with the $j$-th basis vector. Substitution gives the form we shall use repeatedly, $|v\rangle
 =\sum_{i=1}^{d}|b_i\rangle\langle b_i|v\rangle.$

p.src: Classical Alternatives and Quantum Superpositions

u.src: Classical Alternatives and Quantum Superpositions
en: Classical Alternatives and Quantum Superpositions

p.src: We can now attach physical meaning to the vector space. A classical phase space is a set of possible states. Subsets support the ordinary logic of union and intersection, OR and AND. Quantum states carry additional linear structure. Adding two state vectors and multiplying them by complex numbers can produce another physical state; mere set membership cannot express this.

p.src:
Begin with a coin. Its classically distinguishable configurations are heads and tails. We may call them $H$ and $T$, or label them $+1$ and $-1$, but those labels are names, not vector lengths. The quantum model assigns orthonormal states $\langle H|H\rangle=\langle T|T\rangle=1,
 \qquad
 \langle H|T\rangle=0.$ The real physical example behind the coin is an electron with two distinguishable spin outcomes.

p.src: The orthogonality has operational content. Configurations that one ideal measurement can distinguish with certainty are represented by orthogonal vectors. This is one of the postulates we shall use. For a six-sided die, the same rule gives six states $|1\rangle,\ldots,|6\rangle$ satisfying $\langle i|j\rangle=\delta_{ij}.$

p.src: Now comes the step that has no classical analogue: $|C\rangle=\alpha_H|H\rangle+\alpha_T|T\rangle.$ This ’confused coin’ is a genuine quantum state, neither heads nor tails. It is a coherent superposition, not a classical statistical mixture whose member secretly has one definite face. Likewise, $|D\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{6}\alpha_i|i\rangle$ is a superposition of the six die outcomes.

p.src: Amplitudes, Probabilities, and Normalization

u.src: Amplitudes, Probabilities, and Normalization
en: Amplitudes, Probabilities, and Normalization

p.src:
If all outcomes are accounted for, their probabilities add to one: $|\alpha_H|^2+|\alpha_T|^2=1.$ Using Eq. , this is precisely $\langle C|C\rangle=1.$ For the die, $\sum_{i=1}^{6}|\alpha_i|^2=1,
 \qquad
 \langle D|D\rangle=1.$ Physical state vectors are therefore normalized.

p.src: The First Look at Operators

u.src: The First Look at Operators
en: The First Look at Operators

p.src: There is one more mathematical object to introduce. An operation assigns a new vector to every vector in the space. Fixed-angle rotation, uniform rescaling, and reflection about an axis are familiar examples. Squaring a vector’s length is also an operation, but it is not linear: a vector of length $2$ is sent to one of length $4$, while a vector of length $3$ is sent to one of length $9$.

p.src:
We denote a linear operator by a hatted letter, such as $\hat L$. It obeys homogeneity and additivity: $\begin{aligned}
 \hat L\bigl(\alpha|A\rangle\bigr)
 &=\alpha\,\hat L|A\rangle,\\
 \hat L\bigl(|A\rangle+|B\rangle\bigr)
 &=\hat L|A\rangle+\hat L|B\rangle.
 \end{aligned}$ Equivalently, for arbitrary complex $\alpha,\beta$, $\hat L\bigl(\alpha|A\rangle+\beta|B\rangle\bigr)
 =\alpha\hat L|A\rangle+\beta\hat L|B\rangle.$

p.src: The two defining rules for a linear operator: scalar multiplication passes through the operator, and the image of a sum is the sum of the images.

p.src: Rotation by a fixed angle passes both tests. Rotating twice a vector gives twice the rotated vector. If $\mathbf a+\mathbf b$ is the diagonal of a parallelogram, rotating the whole parallelogram shows $R(\mathbf a+\mathbf b)=R\mathbf a+R\mathbf b.$ Uniform doubling and reflection are linear for the same reason. The length-squaring operation fails: scaling the input by $\alpha$ changes the length squared by $|\alpha|^2$, not by $\alpha$.

p.src: State vectors describe the possible states of a quantum system. Linear operators will describe measurable quantities, or observables: the quantum version of asking whether the coin is heads or tails. The precise relation between an observable, its operator, and the outcomes of a measurement is the next step. We are now close enough to the formalism to begin making predictions.
